guide.title: Infectious Disease & Sepsis
guide.lead: Sepsis is infection plus failing organs, and it kills when it's caught late. Look for it in every patient with an infection who seems "off". Screen, start treatment, pre-alert the hospital, and protect yourself with the right precautions.

sections.title: Could this be sepsis?
sections.question: Suspected infection plus any sign of organ trouble?
items: Respiratory rate 22 or more; SpO₂ falling
Systolic 100 mmHg or less; mottled or cold skin
Little urine; temperature above 38 °C or below 36 °C
sections.yes: Sepsis alert: oxygen to SpO₂ 94–98%, IV access and fluids per protocol, pre-alert, rapid transport. Antibiotics within 1 hour for shock or probable sepsis.
sections.no: Keep reassessing: sepsis can develop over hours.

sections.title: Screening tools
rows: 2 or more of: respiratory rate 22 or more, systolic 100 mmHg or less, altered mentation
Not to be used alone: misses many cases
5 or more; 7 or more is high risk
Uses the full set of vital signs
Temperature above 38 °C or below 36 °C, heart rate above 90/min, respiratory rate above 20/min
notes: Septic shock: needs vasopressors to keep MAP 65 mmHg or more, with lactate above 2 mmol/L, despite fluids.
Fluids: at least 30 mL/kg within 3 hours for hypotension; smaller boluses with heart failure.

sections.title: Protect yourself
rows: Gloves; eye protection for splashes; hand hygiene
Gown and gloves; soap and water for C. difficile
Surgical mask on you and the patient
N95 or better; mask the patient; fresh-air ventilation

sections.title: High-risk patients
items: Non-blanching rash with fever: meningococcal sepsis

quiz.q: A nursing home resident with a smelly urine has confusion, RR 24, BP 98/62, temperature 38.9 °C. Interpretation?
options: Suspected sepsis: qSOFA 3, rapid transport and pre-alert
quiz.explanation: All three qSOFA criteria are present.

quiz.q: Spreading leg cellulitis with confusion; after 500 mL of fluid, BP falls from 104/68 to 92/56. This suggests:

options: Respiratory rate 22 or more, systolic 100 mmHg or less, altered mentation
Heart rate above 90, temperature above 38 °C, white count
quiz.explanation: 2 or more is high risk, but don't use it alone to rule sepsis out.

options: Vasopressors needed for MAP 65 mmHg or more and lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids

quiz.explanation: Smaller boluses with heart failure; reassess.
Surgical mask on you and the patient.

quiz.explanation: Pre-alerting helps the hospital start early.

flashcards.question: qSOFA
flashcards.answer: Respiratory rate 22 or more, systolic 100 mmHg or less, altered mentation. 2 or more is high risk; not to be used alone as a screen.

flashcards.question: SIRS criteria
flashcards.answer: Temperature above 38 °C or below 36 °C, heart rate above 90/min, respiratory rate above 20/min, abnormal white count.

flashcards.question: Septic shock
flashcards.answer: Sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP 65 mmHg or more, with lactate above 2 mmol/L, despite fluids.

flashcards.question: Common sources of sepsis
flashcards.answer: Lungs (pneumonia), urine, abdomen, skin and soft tissue.

flashcards.question: Airborne precautions
flashcards.answer: Tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox: N95 or better; mask the patient.

flashcards.question: C. difficile hand hygiene
flashcards.answer: Soap and water: alcohol rub doesn't kill the spores.

flashcards.question: Meningococcal disease
flashcards.answer: Fever, stiff neck, headache, confusion, photophobia, non-blanching rash. Droplet precautions.

flashcards.question: EMS care in sepsis
flashcards.answer: Screen (NEWS2, qSOFA, judgement), oxygen to 94–98%, IV fluids per protocol, monitor, pre-alert, rapid transport.

critical.scenario: A 68-year-old with COPD and diabetes: green sputum for 3 days, confused for 6 hours. HR 118, BP 104/70, RR 26, SpO₂ 89%, temperature 39.4 °C, right basal crackles.
critical.question: Diagnosis and priority?

options.t: Pneumonia with sepsis: oxygen to target, fluids per protocol, monitor closely, pre-alert, rapid transport

options.f: Fever, focal crackles and confusion point to pneumonia with sepsis.

critical.explanation: A sepsis pre-alert lets the hospital start antibiotics early.
critical.kpi: Recognises sepsis using qSOFA in a patient with pneumonia

critical.scenario: A 19-year-old student: severe headache, fever 40.1 °C, vomiting, stiff neck, lethargic. Purple non-blanching spots on her trunk and legs.
critical.question: Diagnosis and precautions?

options.t: Meningococcal meningitis and sepsis: droplet precautions (mask her and yourself), oxygen, rapid transport, pre-alert

options.f: A non-blanching rash means meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.
Droplet is the requirement; an N95 also protects.

critical.explanation: Exposed crew may need prophylactic antibiotics.
critical.kpi: Identifies meningococcal meningitis and applies appropriate droplet precautions

critical.scenario: At a shelter, a 55-year-old has coughed for 6 weeks with night sweats, weight loss and blood-streaked sputum. Temperature 38.5 °C, SpO₂ 92%.
critical.question: Likely diagnosis and precautions?

options.t: Active tuberculosis: N95 for you, surgical mask on the patient, oxygen to target, fresh-air ventilation, pre-alert for isolation

options.f: This history is TB until proven otherwise.

critical.kpi: Recognises tuberculosis and applies appropriate airborne precautions
